title: Schedules and polling

story: You assign RH-1234 to Nova. How does Nova even learn about it? Jira can call a URL of ours when something changes, which is called a webhook. But the orchestrator lives in a private network that nothing on the internet can reach, and we want to keep it that way. So we reverse the direction: every minute, we ask Jira which tickets are assigned to Nova.

"Every minute" sounds simple until Jira is slow. One Tuesday a search takes three minutes instead of two seconds, and a simple timer would start a second poll and then a third while the first is still running, all asking the slow Jira the same question. And after a night when the orchestrator was down for two hours, a simple scheduler might run all 120 missed polls the moment it comes back.
hook.question: How do we ask Jira every minute without polls overlapping, and without a flood of polls after an outage?

read.h: Why we ask Jira instead of letting Jira call us
p: A webhook is a public door. Jira would call a URL of ours, so that URL must be reachable from the internet, and every request to it would have to prove that it really came from Jira. Polling closes that door: we call Jira, and nothing on the internet calls us. The price is a delay of up to a minute, which nobody notices on a ticket that runs for hours.

Polling is also simple to make safe, because of the previous lesson. The poll finds RH-1234 again every minute for as long as it is assigned to Nova, and each time it calls startRun, which names the run nova:RH-1234 and joins the open run. So a poll can never start a second run for the same ticket, and finding a ticket twice costs nothing.

The poll is split the usual way. A tiny workflow, pollJira, calls one activity, startMatches, which does the real work: it searches Jira and starts or joins one run per ticket. If Jira is down, the activity fails and its retry policy tries again later; nothing else breaks.

notes.text: SHORT options with the retry policy for people's tools: if Jira is down, try again with growing waits.
A registry holds one entry per Jira query: Nova's, and later one for bug tickets. Each entry has a name, an agent, the JQL and how often to run.
startRun names the run nova:RH-1234 and joins it if it is open, so the same ticket found every minute still has one run.

read.h: A schedule: when, what, and two rules
p: Something must start pollJira every minute. We do not write a loop for that; we create a Temporal schedule. A schedule is an object stored in the Temporal Service that starts a workflow at set times. It has an ID, such as poll-jira-nova, a spec that says when (an interval like every 1 minute, or a cron expression), and an action that says what to start: which workflow, with which arguments, on which task queue. Each run it starts gets the action's workflow ID with the time of the tick added, for example poll-jira-nova-2026-10-15T23:12:20Z.

A schedule also has policies, two rules for the bad days from the story. The overlap policy decides what a tick does when the run from the last tick is still going. The catch-up window decides how old a missed tick may be and still run after an outage. The next section explains both.

The code creates the schedule when the worker starts. A second worker, or the next deploy, runs the same code, and create would fail with ScheduleAlreadyRunning, so the code updates the existing schedule instead. That makes it safe to run as often as you like.

notes.text: poll-jira-nova for Nova's entry. One schedule per Jira query.
When: every 1 minute for Nova, every 5 minutes for bugs.
What: start pollJira with the query's name, on the orchestrator's own queue.
The two rules: never start a poll while the last one runs, and forget ticks older than one interval.
The schedule already exists, from an earlier start. Update it, so a changed interval or JQL takes effect.

read.h: When a tick finds the last poll still running
p: Back to the slow Tuesday. The overlap policy has six options, and three show the choice well. SKIP drops the tick: if the last poll is still running, this tick starts nothing, and the next poll starts at the first tick after the slow one finished. ALLOW_ALL starts a new poll anyway, so slow polls overlap on a slow Jira, which is exactly when Jira needs fewer requests. BUFFER_ONE keeps one waiting tick and runs it right after the slow poll. The other three are BUFFER_ALL, which keeps every waiting tick and runs them one after another, and CANCEL_OTHER and TERMINATE_OTHER, which stop the running poll to make room for the new one. For a poll SKIP is right, because a poll that starts a few seconds later finds the same tickets anyway. SKIP is also the default.
In the lab, Jira answers in 25 seconds and the schedule ticks every 10. You can see SKIP at work: a poll starts every 30 seconds, never two at once, and the schedule counts the ticks it dropped.

The catch-up window handles the night of the outage. When the Temporal Service comes back, it looks at the ticks it missed and runs only the ones younger than the window. Its default is a whole year, so after a long outage a schedule would still try to run ticks that are hours old. With a window as long as the interval, one minute, a two-hour outage costs us at most one late poll, and the next normal tick does the rest.

deeper.h: Go deeper: cron schedules for the routines
p: Routines are agents like Nova that start from an event or a clock instead of an assignment. The daily and weekly ones, such as the routine that looks for dead frontend code, start from schedules with a cron expression instead of an interval. A cron expression has five fields: minute, hour, day of the month, month and day of the week. "17 4 * * 0-4" means 04:17 from Sunday to Thursday, our working week, in the time zone Asia/Jerusalem.

The minutes are odd on purpose. Many systems start their jobs at 04:00, and starting at 04:17 keeps ours away from that rush. Overlap is SKIP here too, so a slow routine never gets a second copy of itself.

lab.title: One poll at a time
needs: Two terminal tabs, plus the dev server's
lab.goal: Poll a fake Jira from a Temporal schedule, see each ticket join its one open run, and see the overlap policy drop ticks while a slow poll is still running.

guess.q: The schedule ticks every 10 seconds with overlap SKIP. Jira becomes slow and each poll takes 25 seconds. How often does a poll start?

options.text: Every 10 seconds, so two or three polls run at once.
options.why: That is ALLOW_ALL. SKIP never starts a poll while the previous one is still running.

options.text: Every 30 seconds: the ticks during a slow poll are dropped, and the next tick after it ends starts a new one.
options.why: A poll runs from :20 to :45, the ticks at :30 and :40 are skipped, and the tick at :50 starts the next one.

options.text: Every 35 seconds: each poll waits 10 seconds after the last one ended.
options.why: A schedule does not wait after a run. It ticks on its own clock and only decides what to do with each tick.

follow.say: Make a fake Jira: a file with the tickets assigned to Nova and how many seconds a search takes. You will change it while the poll runs.
Write startMatches. It reads the fake Jira, waits as long as the search takes, and starts or joins nova:<ticket> with USE_EXISTING, the way startRun does.
Write the two workflows: pollJira, which the schedule starts, and a small ticketToPr that waits for an approval.
Write the worker. It runs two workers in one process, because the polls run on the orchestrator's queue and the tickets on Nova's.
Start the worker, then open a third tab and create the schedule: every 10 seconds, overlap Skip, catch-up window 10 seconds. The CLI prints nothing when it works.

lab.build: Our platform does not create schedules with the CLI; the worker creates them in code when it starts. Delete the schedule with temporal schedule delete -s poll-jira-nova, then write ensure-schedule.mjs: it creates poll-jira-nova with the same spec, action and policies through client.schedule.create, and when that throws ScheduleAlreadyRunning it updates the existing schedule instead. Run it twice: the first run prints "created poll-jira-nova" and the second "updated poll-jira-nova".
checks: Every poll in the worker tab shows the same run ID for nova:RH-1234.
With searchSeconds at 25, a new poll starts every 30 seconds, never two at once, and temporal schedule describe shows SkippedOverlap above 0.
RH-1235 got its own run the first time the slow poll finished, and kept that same run afterwards.
For your build: node ensure-schedule.mjs prints created the first time and updated the second, and temporal schedule describe -s poll-jira-nova shows OverlapPolicy Skip and CatchupWindow 10s.

At the end, temporal schedule delete -s poll-jira-nova prints Schedule deleted, temporal workflow terminate --query "ExecutionStatus='Running'" --yes stops the ticket runs that are still waiting, and you stopped the worker with Ctrl+C.
lab.fix: A teammate worried that Skip loses polls, so they recreated the schedule with --overlap-policy AllowAll "so no tick is ever dropped". Jira is slow again (searchSeconds 25). Delete the schedule, create it again with AllowAll, wait half a minute and run temporal workflow list --query "WorkflowType='pollJira' AND ExecutionStatus='Running'": two or three polls are running at once, all asking the slow Jira the same question. Explain to the teammate why no work is lost with Skip, and put Skip back.
explain: Why do we poll Jira instead of letting Jira call a webhook of ours?
The poll finds RH-1234 every minute for hours. Why does that never start a second run?
What does the overlap policy SKIP do when Jira is slow, and why is that better than starting a new poll on every tick?
lab.done: Your schedule polled the fake Jira, joined one run per ticket, skipped ticks while a slow poll ran, and was created in code twice without an error; you deleted it and stopped the worker.

check.q: Why does our platform poll Jira every minute instead of receiving a webhook?

options.text: Jira cannot send webhooks to other services
options.why: It can. We choose not to receive them.

options.text: Polling is faster than a webhook
options.why: It is slower: up to a minute of delay. We accept that delay on purpose.

options.text: A webhook needs a URL that the internet can reach; with polling we call Jira and nothing outside can call us
options.why: The orchestrator stays in a private network. A one-minute delay is the price, and on a ticket that runs for hours nobody notices it.

check.q: A Jira search suddenly takes three minutes, and poll-jira-nova ticks every minute with overlap SKIP. What happens?

options.text: The ticks during the slow search are dropped, and the next tick after it finishes starts a new poll
options.why: SKIP never runs two polls at once. The tickets are found by the next poll anyway, so nothing is lost.

options.text: Three polls run at the same time, one per tick
options.why: That is ALLOW_ALL, which sends more and more requests to a Jira that is already slow.

options.text: The schedule pauses itself until someone unpauses it
options.why: A schedule only pauses when someone pauses it, or when it is set to pause after a failure.

check.q: The orchestrator was down for two hours. poll-jira-nova has a catch-up window of one minute. What happens when it comes back?

options.text: All 120 missed polls run, one after the other
options.why: That is what a very long window allows, and its default is a whole year. Our window is one minute.

options.text: Only ticks younger than one minute still run, so polling simply continues
options.why: Older ticks are dropped, and the next poll finds every ticket assigned during the outage anyway.

options.text: The schedule is deleted and must be created again
options.why: Schedules live in the Temporal Service and survive outages; the worker also creates or updates them when it starts.

p: Every Jira trigger uses one mechanism. A registry holds one entry per query: Nova's (tickets assigned to Nova, every minute) and the bug fixers' (triaged bugs, every 5 minutes). When the orchestrator worker starts, ensureSchedules creates or updates one schedule per entry, poll-jira-nova and so on, with overlap SKIP and a catch-up window as long as the interval. Each poll runs on the ai-agents-orchestrator queue and calls startRun for every match.

Nova's entry runs its JQL as the Nova service account, and it also finds the requester, the person who assigned the ticket to Nova; with no requester, it starts nothing. The scheduled routines use cron schedules named sched:<name> in the Asia/Jerusalem time zone. During an incident, DevOps can pause a schedule, and the kill switch in startRun refuses new runs for a stopped agent even if a poll runs.

tickets.why: The query registry, pollJira and startMatches, and ensureSchedules with SKIP and a catch-up window.
Nova's entry: the Nova service account, its JQL every minute, and the requester from the changelog.
The bug-fixer polls every 5 minutes and the cron schedules for the daily and weekly routines.

words.plain: A URL of yours that another service calls when something changes. It must be reachable from outside.
Asking another service again and again whether something changed, instead of waiting to be called.
An object in the Temporal Service that starts a workflow at set times, from an interval or a cron expression.
What a schedule's tick does when the run from the last tick is still going: skip, wait, or start anyway.
How old a missed tick may be and still run after an outage.

review.q: Write the spec, the action and the policies of poll-jira-nova from memory.
review.a: spec: every 1 minute; action: start pollJira with the query name, workflow ID poll-jira-nova, on ai-agents-orchestrator; policies: overlap SKIP and a catch-up window of 1 minute.

review.q: Why does ensureSchedules catch ScheduleAlreadyRunning and update the schedule?
review.a: It runs every time a worker starts, so the schedule usually exists already. Updating it makes the code safe to run any number of times and applies changes to the interval, the JQL or the policies.

review.q: A poll is slow and a tick is skipped. Can a ticket assigned during that time be missed?
review.a: No. The next poll asks Jira again and finds every ticket that is assigned to Nova at that moment; startRun joins runs that already exist.

remember: A schedule starts the poll every minute; SKIP keeps slow polls from overlapping, a short catch-up window stops a flood after an outage, and the workflow ID makes finding a ticket twice harmless.
